G_{m}v_{o2}+(G_{o}+sC_{L})v_{o3}&=G_{p}v_{x}} \tag{9}$$

The $N$ equations (9) are circulant.  The excitation
${\bf G_{p}}v_{x}[1\,1\dots 1]^{T}$ is the ${\bf k}=0$
Fourier vector.  Only the common mode

$$v_{o1}=v_{o2}=\dots =v_{oN}=v_{c}\tag{10}$$

is excited.  Putting $S=\sum v_{ok}=Nv_{c}$ and adding
(9),

$$S\,(G_{m}+G_{o}+sC_{L})=NG_{p}v_{x}\tag{11}$$

$$S=N\,{\dfrac{G_{p}}{G_{m}+G_{o}+sC_{L}}}\,v_{x}\tag{12}$$

and, from (6), for any $k$

$$v_{c}={\dfrac{G_{p}}{G_{m}+G_{o}+sC_{L}}}\,v_{x}\tag{13}$$

The total current furnished by the test generator
$v_{x}$ is the sum of the $N$ $p$ currents.  From (1)
(2)

$$\eqalign{
I_{x}&=\sum_{k}^{N}i_{pk}
      =\sum_{k}^{N}\left[ G_{p}v_{x}-g_{mp}v_{ik}-g_{op}v_{ok}\right]\cr
     &=NG_{p}v_{x}-G_{p}S\tag{14}}$$

because $\sum v_{ik}=\sum v_{ok}=S$.  With (12)

$$I_{x}=NG_{p}v_{x}\left[1-{\dfrac{G_{p}}
{G_{m}+G_{o}+sC_{L}}}\right] \tag{15}$$

so that the closed loop admittance seen at the common
$V_{DD}$ rail is, for $N$ stages,

$$Y_{x}(s)={{I_{x}}\over {v_{x}}}
      =N\,G_{p}\,{{G_{m}+G_{o}-G_{p}+sC_{L}}\over 
            {G_{m}+G_{o}+sC_{L}}}\tag{16}$$

and, since $G_{m}+G_{o}-G_{p}=g_{mn}+g_{on}$,

$$Y_{x}(s)=N\,(g_{mp}+g_{op})\,
     {{g_{mn}+g_{on}+sC_{L}}\over 
      {g_{mn}+g_{mp}+g_{on}+g_{op}+sC_{L}}}\tag{17}$$

$$Z_{x}(s)=Y_{x}^{-1}(s)\tag{18}$$

is a conventional $R\parallel C$ impedance with a
pole

$$\omega _{p}={{G_{m}+G_{o}}\over {C_{L}}}\tag{19}$$

and a zero

$$\omega _{z}={{g_{mn}+g_{on}}\over {C_{L}}}\tag{20}$$

$\omega _{p}$ is, to within $G_{o}$, the ``oscillation''
pole

$$s_{1,2}={{-\,G_{o}+G_{m}/2\pm j{{\sqrt{3}}\over {2}}G_{m}}
      \over {C_{L}}}\tag{21}$$

of the linearised metastable point, i. e. 
${\rm Im}\,s_{1,2}= \omega _{osc}\approx {{\sqrt{3}}G_{m}/
2C_{L}}$.

In particular, for $|s|C_{L}\ll G_{m}$, the normal low
frequency, $d-c$, resistance is

$$R_{x0}=Y_{x}^{-1}(0)={{G_{m}+G_{o}}\over 
            {NG_{p}(g_{mn}+g_{on})}}\tag{22}$$

$$R_{x0}={1\over N}
      {{g_{mn}+g_{mp}+g_{on}+g_{op}}\over 
       {(g_{mp}+g_{op})(g_{mn}+g_{on})}}\tag{23}$$

With the passive sign convention, $I_{x}$ into the
circuit, $R_{x0}>0$.  With the generator sign convention
normally used in oscillator theory, $I_{x}$ out of the
circuit, $R_{x0}<0$.  Neglecting channel length
modulation, $g_{o}\to 0$,

$$R_{x0}={1\over N}\left({1\over {g_{mn}}}+{1\over {g_{mp}}}
      \right) \tag{24}$$

For the conventional symmetric design $g_{mn}=g_{mp}=g_{m}$

$$|R_{x0}|\approx {2\over {Ng_{m}}}\tag{25}$$

so that for the three stage ring in the figure

$$|R_{x0}|\approx {2\over {3g_{m}}}\approx {1\over {g_{m}}}
\;\;{\rm to\;within\;a\;factor\;2}\tag{26}$$

in the generator convention

$$R_{x0}\approx -{2\over {3g_{m}}}\tag{27}$$

often quoted simply as $R_{x}\approx -1/g_{m}$ or
$|R_{x}|\approx 1/g_{m}$.  Keeping $g_{o}=1/r_{o}$,

$$R_{x0}={2\over {3g_{m}}}{1\over {1+g_{o}/g_{m}}}
      \approx {2\over {3g_{m}}}\left(1-{1\over {g_{m}r_{o}}}
      \right)\tag{28}$$

and in general $|R_{x}|\sim 50-500\,{\rm \Omega}$ for a
normal $g_{m}\sim 1-10\,{\rm mS}$ per device.

Well above the common mode pole, $|s|C_{L}\gg G_{m}$,

$$Y_{x}(\infty )=NG_{p}\approx Ng_{mp}\tag{29}$$

$$|R_{x\infty }|\approx {1\over {Ng_{mp}}}\to {1\over 
      {3g_{m}}}\;\;{\rm sym.}\tag{30}$$

so that, up to the $2\times $ factor,

$$|Z_{x}(s)|\approx |R_{x0}|{{1+s/\omega _{z}}\over 
       {1+s/\omega _{p}}}\tag{31}$$

goes from $\approx 2/3g_{m}$ at $d-c$ to $\approx
1/3g_{m}$ for $\omega \gg \omega _{p}$ with
${\rm Re}\,Z_{x}>0$ for the passive reference arrow.
The magnitude at the (small signal) oscillation
frequency $s=j\omega _{osc}$ is the same order of
magnitude,

$$Y_{x}(j\omega _{osc})\approx Ng_{mp}
      {{1+j\omega _{osc}/\omega _{z}}\over 
       {1+j\omega _{osc}/\omega _{p}}}\tag{32}$$

with ${\rm Re}\,Y_{x}>0$.

Any expression of the form $R_{x}\sim 1/Ng_{m}$ to
$2/Ng_{m}$ i. e. $R_{x}\sim 1/g_{m}$ in order of
magnitude is accepted as correct.  With the bulk effect
included $g_{mp}\to g_{mp}+g_{mbp}$.

Time averaged over the large signal limit cycle the
circuit draws on the average

$$I_{DD,av}\approx N\,C_{L}V_{DD}f_{osc}\approx 
      {{N\,I_{Dsat}}\over 2}\tag{33}$$

so that the large signal, $V_{DD}$ to $I_{DD,av}$,
resistance is

$$R_{x,LS}={{V_{DD}}\over {I_{DD,av}}}\approx 
      {{2V_{DD}}\over {NI_{Dsat}}}\approx {{R_{on,p}}\over N}
      \approx {1\over {N\mu _{p}C_{ox}(W/L)_{p}
      (V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|)}}\tag{34}$$

again a few $10\,{\rm \Omega}$ to a few $100\,{\rm \Omega}$
per stage, positive in the passive convention, negative
in the generator convention.  E. g. $g_{m}=2\,{\rm mS}$,
$|R_{x0}|\approx 330\,{\rm \Omega}$, 
$|R_{x\infty }|\approx 170\,{\rm \Omega}$;
$g_{m}=5\,{\rm mS}$, $|R_{x0}|\approx 130\,{\rm \Omega}$,
etc.  In round numbers the supply sees a low impedance
$\sim 1/g_{m}$ to ground which, as an active impedance,
is normally written with a minus sign, $Z_{x}\approx
-1/g_{m}$.  Closing $Z_{x}$ on an inductor
$L_{x}=1/\omega _{osc}^{2}C_{x}$ gives the familiar
supply tuned $LC$ VCO.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The limit-cycle relation I_DD,av ≈ N C_L V_DD f_osc and R = V_DD/I_DD,av imply R ≈ 1/(N C_L f_osc), or 1/(3 C_L f_0) for this ring, matching the full-credit rule. The metastable g_m analysis is extraneous, but the correct oscillation-driven capacitive mechanism and resistance form are present.

answer.text:
With the usual ``metastable'' linearisation the
${\rm V}_{DD}$ node is a common mode node.
Put ${\rm V}_{DD}={\rm V}_{x}+v_{x}$ , $v_{o_{i}}$
the small signal output of the $i$th. inverter, Fig.1,
${\rm C}$ the total capacitance on the node, ${\rm W}$ the
$p$ device ${\rm S}$, ${\rm G}$, ${\rm D}$ $={\rm V}_{x}$,
$v_{i}$, $v_{o}$ and the $n$ device ${\rm G}$, ${\rm D}$,
${\rm S}$ $=v_{i},v_{o},0$.

$${\eqalign{
i_{Dp}&=g_{mp}(v_{x}-v_{i})+g_{op}(v_{x}-v_{o})\cr
i_{Dn}&=g_{mn}v_{i}+g_{on}v_{o}\cr}} \tag{1}$$

$${\rm KCL}_{o}:\;i_{Dp}=i_{Dn}+sCv_{o}\tag{2}$$

so that with

$$\eqalign{
A&=g_{mp}+g_{op}\cr
B&=g_{mp}+g_{mn}\cr
C_{0}&=g_{op}+g_{on}\cr
C(s)&=C_{0}+sC\cr}\tag{3}$$

$$\,A\,v_{x}=Bv_{i}+C(s)v_{o}\,\tag{4}$$

and, for the closed loop,

$$\eqalign{
C(s)v_{o1}+Bv_{o3}&=Av_{x}\cr
Bv_{o1}+C(s)v_{o2}&=Av_{x}\cr
Bv_{o2}+C(s)v_{o3}&=Av_{x}\cr}\tag{5}$$

whose determinant is $C^{3}+B^{3}\ne 0$.
For the common mode excitation $v_{x}{\bf 1}$ the
symmetric solution

$$v_{o1}=v_{o2}=v_{o3}=v_{o}={A\over {B+C(s)}}v_{x}\tag{6}$$

satisfies (5).

$${v_{o}\over {v_{x}}}\approx {{g_{mp}}\over
{g_{mp}+g_{mn}}}\approx {1\over 2}\qquad g_{o}\ll g_{m} \tag{7}$$

the conventional small signal inverter supply to output
{\it positive} gain.  The small signal current taken from
the $v_{x}$ source is the sum of the three $p$ source
currents

$$\eqalign{
i_{x}&=\sum_{1}^{3}i_{Dpi}
      =\sum_{1}^{3}\left[ A\,v_{x}-g_{mp}v_{i}-g_{op}v_{o}\right] 
       =3Av_{x}-3Av_{o}\cr
     &=3A\left[1-{A\over {B+C(s)}}\right]v_{x}
      =3A{{B+C(s)-A}\over {B+C(s)}}v_{x} \cr
     &=3A{{g_{mn}+g_{on}+sC}\over {B+C(s)}}v_{x} \tag{8}}$$

so that, in the low frequency metastable bias, the small
signal impedance seen looking into the common ${\rm V}_{DD}$
rail is

$$\eqalign{
Z_{x}(s)&={v_{x}\over {i_{x}}}
        ={1\over {3A}}{{B+C(s)}\over {g_{mn}+g_{on}+sC}}\cr
        &={{g_{mn}+g_{mp}+g_{on}+g_{op}+sC}\over
                {3(g_{mp}+g_{op})(g_{mn}+g_{on}+sC)}} \tag{9}}$$

I. e. the ${\rm V}_{DD}$ node sees three diode connected
inverters in parallel.  At $s=0$

$$R_{x0}=Z_{x}(0)={{B+C_{0}}\over {3A(g_{mn}+g_{on})}}
      ={{g_{mn}+g_{mp}+g_{on}+g_{op}}\over
             {3(g_{mp}+g_{op})(g_{mn}+g_{on})}} \tag{10}$$

$${R_{x0}={1\over 3}\left[{1\over {g_{mn}+g_{on}}}+
                 {1\over {g_{mp}+g_{op}}}\right] } \tag{11}$$

in parallel with $r_{on}\Vert r_{op}$.
For $g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$

$$\;R_{x0}\approx {1\over 3}\left({1\over {g_{mn}}}+{1\over
{g_{mp}}}\right)={{g_{mn}+g_{mp}}\over {3g_{mn}g_{mp}}}\; \tag{12}$$

If the inverter transconductance is put $G_{m}=g_{mn}+
g_{mp}$, (12) is $R_{x0}\approx 1/3G_{m}$ per stage.
For the conventional symmetric bias
$g_{mn}=g_{mp}=g_{m}$, $g_{o}\to 0$,

$$R_{x0}\approx {2\over {3g_{m}}}={4\over {3G_{m}}}\approx
{1\over {3g_{m}}}{\rm \;\;per\;side}\tag{13}$$

positive with the passive sign convention, i.{\rm e.}
$|R_{x}|\sim g_{m}^{-1}$, normally a few $10^{2}{\rm \Omega}$,
e. {\rm g.} $g_{m}=1\,{\rm mA/V}$, $R_{x0}\approx 0.66\,{\rm k\Omega}
\approx 0.33\,{\rm k\Omega}$ per $g_{m}$.

With the oscillator large signal active sign convention the
same magnitude is normally quoted as a negative resistance,

$$|R_{x}|\approx {1\over {N\,g_{m}}}\approx {1\over {3g_{m}}}
\;\;{\rm per\;device,}\;\;|R_{x}|\approx {2\over {3g_{m}}}
\approx {1\over {G_{m}}}{\rm \;for\;the\;CMOS\;inverter,} \tag{14}$$

so that, e. {\rm g.}

$$R_{x}\approx -\,{1\over {3g_{m}}}\;\;{\rm to}\;\;-{2\over {3g_{m}}}
\approx -\,{1\over {G_{m}}}\tag{15}$$

in the $g_{o}\to 0$ square law form, and, retaining
$r_{o}=1/g_{o}$,

$$R_{x}\approx -\,{{(g_{m}r_{o})^{2}}\over {3g_{m}}}\approx
-\,{r_{o}\over 3}\tag{16}$$

at the oscillation frequency, ${\rm Re}\,Z_{x}(j\omega _{{\rm
osc}})<0$, $|\,{\rm Re}\,Z_{x}(j\omega _{{\rm osc}})\,|
\approx r_{o}/3\sim g_{m}^{-1}$.

In round numbers the ${\rm V}_{DD}$ node looks like
$N=3$ diode connected inverters in parallel, i. {\rm e.}
like a resistance $\sim 1/G_{m}$ to ground, normally quoted
simply as $|R_{x}|\sim 1/g_{m}$, more precisely (11)--(13).
With the passive reference direction $R_{x}>0$; with the
usual negative resistance oscillator convention
$R_{x}\approx -|R_{x}|$.  Any of the equivalent forms
(9)--(15) is acceptable; e. {\rm g.} for $r_{o}\to \infty $

$$Z_{x}(s)\approx {1\over 3}{1\over {g_{mp}}}
{{g_{mp}+g_{mn}+sC}\over {g_{mn}+sC}}\approx
{2/3g_{m}}\,{1\over {1+sC/g_{m}}}$$

for $g_{mn}=g_{mp}=g_{m}$, so that $Z_{x}(0)\approx
2/3g_{m}\approx 1/3G_{m}$ and $|Z_{x}(j\omega _{{\rm osc}})|
\approx 1/g_{m}$ negative in the active convention.  For
hand calculation $|R_{x}|\approx 1/3g_{m}\approx 1/G_{m}$
is often quoted, i. {\rm e.} $R_{x}\approx -1/g_{m}$ in
magnitude, $\approx -1/3g_{m}$ per stage.  The $+$
sign is the conventional passive small signal resistance.

answer.text:
Apply a small change $V_{x}$ to the common supply and
let $V_{o1},V_{o2},V_{o3}$ be the resulting changes at the
oscillator nodes. Put the circuit at the high gain
meta-stable point and linearize each inverter.

For one inverter let the input change be $V_{i}$,
the output change be $V_{o}$. NMOS: source ac ground.
PMOS: source $V_{x}$.

Small signal NMOS drain current into the drain:

$$i_{dn}=g_{mn}V_{i}+g_{dsn}V_{o}$$

leaving the output node.

Small signal PMOS source to drain current:

$$i_{sdp}=g_{mp}v_{sg}+g_{dsp}v_{sd}
 =g_{mp}(V_{x}-V_{i})+g_{dsp}(V_{x}-V_{o})$$

entering the output node. Bulk of PMOS is to $V_{x}$,
so $v_{sb}=0$.

KCL at the output, no other ac load,

$$i_{dn}-i_{sdp}=0$$

i.e.

$$g_{mn}V_{i}+g_{dsn}V_{o}=g_{mp}(V_{x}-V_{i})
 +g_{dsp}(V_{x}-V_{o}).$$

Put

$$\begin{aligned}
g_{m}&=g_{mn}+g_{mp}\\
g_{o}&=g_{dsn}+g_{dsp}\\
g_{n}&=g_{mn}+g_{dsn}\\
g_{p}&=g_{mp}+g_{dsp}
\end{aligned}$$

Then for each inverter

$$g_{m}V_{i}+g_{o}V_{o}=g_{p}V_{x} \tag{1}$$
$$V_{o}= \frac{g_{p}}{g_{o}}V_{x}-\frac{g_{m}}{g_{o}}V_{i}.$$

For the 3-stage ring

$$\begin{aligned}
g_{m}V_{o3}+g_{o}V_{o1}&=g_{p}V_{x}\\
g_{m}V_{o1}+g_{o}V_{o2}&=g_{p}V_{x}\\
g_{m}V_{o2}+g_{o}V_{o3}&=g_{p}V_{x}
\end{aligned}$$

The excitation is common to all three identical stages.
The linear system is non-singular, so the solution is
symmetric:

$$V_{o1}=V_{o2}=V_{o3}=V_{o}.$$

Then from (1) with $V_{i}=V_{o}$,

$$(g_{m}+g_{o})V_{o}=g_{p}V_{x},$$

$$V_{o}=\frac{g_{p}}{g_{m}+g_{o}}V_{x}.$$

In other words for supply variations each inverter
has $V_{i}=V_{o}$, i.e. is diode-connected.

The ac current entering the PMOS source, i.e. leaving
the $V_{x}$ node into one inverter, is $i_{sdp}$:

$$I_{1}=g_{mp}(V_{x}-V_{i})+g_{dsp}(V_{x}-V_{o}).$$

Hence for the 3 inverters total current leaving $V_{x}$:

$$I_{x}= \sum_{k=1}^{3}\left[g_{p}V_{x}-g_{mp}V_{ik}
 -g_{dsp}V_{ok}\right].$$

With $V_{ik}=V_{ok}=V_{o}$,

$$I_{x}=3\left[g_{p}V_{x}-(g_{mp}+g_{dsp})V_{o}\right]
 =3g_{p}(V_{x}-V_{o}).$$

$$V_{x}-V_{o}=V_{x}\left[1-\frac{g_{p}}{g_{m}+g_{o}}\right]
 =V_{x}\frac{g_{n}}{g_{m}+g_{o}},$$

since $g_{m}+g_{o}-g_{p}=g_{mn}+g_{dsn}=g_{n}$.

Thus

$$I_{x}=3\frac{g_{p}g_{n}}{g_{m}+g_{o}}V_{x}.$$

The low frequency impedance is three diode-connected
inverters in parallel:

$$R_{x}=\frac{g_{m}+g_{o}}{3\,g_{n}g_{p}}
 =\frac{1}{3}\frac{g_{mn}+g_{mp}+g_{dsn}+g_{dsp}}
 {(g_{mn}+g_{dsn})(g_{mp}+g_{dsp})}.$$

With $g_{ds}\ll g_{m}$,

$$R_{x}\approx \frac{g_{mn}+g_{mp}}{3g_{mn}g_{mp}}
 =\frac13\left(\frac1{g_{mn}}+\frac1{g_{mp}}\right).$$

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The derivation is internally consistent for a static, linearized operating point, but it misses the dominant oscillation-driven charging and discharging of the load capacitances. The resulting gm-based resistance is the static analysis that the golden solution identifies as a major miss.

answer.text:
For one CMOS inverter let in small signal

* NMOS: $g_{mn},\,g_{dn}$ , source ac ground
* PMOS: $g_{mp},\,g_{dp}$ , source the common
$V_{DD}$ node, $n$-well to $V_{DD}$

Put a test source $V_{x}$ on the common $V_{DD}$
node. Let the three inverter input-output voltages be

$$ V_{a},V_{b},V_{c} $$

with

$$\begin{aligned}
1:&\; in=V_{a},\;out=V_{b}\\
2:&\; in=V_{b},\;out=V_{c}\\
3:&\; in=V_{c},\;out=V_{a}
\end{aligned}$$

For inverter $i$ with $in=V_{ini}$, $out=V_{outi}$,

NMOS drain current into drain:

$$ g_{mn}V_{ini}+g_{dn}V_{outi} $$

PMOS source to drain current:

$$ g_{mp}(V_{x}-V_{ini})+g_{dp}(V_{x}-V_{outi}) $$

with $v_{sbp}=0$.  KCL at the output, neglecting
caps, gives

$$g_{mp}(V_{x}-V_{ini})+g_{dp}(V_{x}-V_{outi})
 = g_{mn}V_{ini}+g_{dn}V_{outi}.$$

Put

$$\begin{aligned}
g_{m}&=g_{mn}+g_{mp}\\
g_{o}&=g_{dn}+g_{dp}\\
g_{p}&=g_{mp}+g_{dp}\\
g_{n}&=g_{mn}+g_{dn}
\end{aligned}$$

Then

$$ g_{o}V_{outi}+g_{m}V_{ini}=g_{p}V_{x}. \tag{1}$$

Hence:

$$\begin{aligned}
g_{m}V_{a}+g_{o}V_{b}&=g_{p}V_{x}\\
g_{m}V_{b}+g_{o}V_{c}&=g_{p}V_{x}\\
g_{o}V_{a}+g_{m}V_{c}&=g_{p}V_{x}
\end{aligned}\tag{2}$$

i.e.

$$\begin{bmatrix}
g_{m} & g_{o} & 0\\
0 & g_{m} & g_{o}\\
g_{o} & 0 & g_{m}
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}V_{a}\\V_{b}\\V_{c}\end{bmatrix}
=g_{p}V_{x}\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{bmatrix}.$$

$\det = g_{m}^{3}+g_{o}^{3}\ne 0$. The excitation
is common mode, the circuit is 3-fold symmetric.
Indeed

$$V_{a}=V_{b}=V_{c}=V$$

satisfies (2) with

$$(g_{m}+g_{o})V = g_{p}V_{x},$$

i.e.

$$V = \frac{g_{p}}{g_{m}+g_{o}}V_{x}. \tag{3}$$

By uniqueness this is the solution. For this
common mode excitation each inverter has in ac

$$V_{in}=V_{out},$$

i.e. it is diode connected.

The current drawn from $V_{x}$ by inverter $i$ is
the PMOS source current:

$$I_{si}=g_{mp}(V_{x}-V_{ini})+g_{dp}(V_{x}-V_{outi})
 =g_{p}V_{x}-g_{mp}V_{ini}-g_{dp}V_{outi}.$$

Summing the three stages,

$$\begin{aligned}
I_{x}&=\sum_{i}I_{si}\\
&=3g_{p}V_{x}-(g_{mp}+g_{dp})(V_{a}+V_{b}+V_{c})\\
&=3g_{p}(V_{x}-V).
\end{aligned}$$

With (3),

$$I_{x}=3g_{p}\left(1-\frac{g_{p}}{g_{m}+g_{o}}\right)V_{x}.$$

But $g_{m}+g_{o}-g_{p}=g_{mn}+g_{dn}=g_{n}$. So

$$I_{x}=3\,\frac{g_{p}g_{n}}{g_{m}+g_{o}}V_{x}.$$

The low frequency driving point admittance is
stable, the unstable complex poles are differential
and have zero sum, so are not excited. Hence

$$R_{x}=\frac{V_{x}}{I_{x}}=\frac{g_{m}+g_{o}}{3g_{p}g_{n}}.$$

i.e.

$$ R_{x}=\frac{1}{3}\,
\frac{g_{mn}+g_{mp}+g_{dn}+g_{dp}}
{(g_{mn}+g_{dn})(g_{mp}+g_{dp})} $$

Each diode connected inverter is $\approx 1/g_{mn}+
1/g_{mp}$ from $V_{DD}$ to ground, three in parallel.
Neglecting $g_{d}$,

$$R_{x}\approx \frac{g_{mn}+g_{mp}}{3g_{mn}g_{mp}}
 =\frac13\left(\frac1{g_{mn}}+\frac1{g_{mp}}\right).$$

In particular for $g_{mn}=g_{mp}=g_{m}$, $R_{x}\approx 2/3g_{m}$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The derivation analyzes a static common-mode operating point and obtains a gm-based diode-connected resistance, but misses the dominant oscillation-driven charging and discharging of the node capacitances. The expected resistance is approximately 1/(3 f0 CL), not the static gm-based result.

answer.text:
By symmetry all of the stages respond identically to a
perturbation on the common $V_{DD}$.

Put a small signal $V_{x}$ on the common supply and let
$V_{1},V_{2},V_{3}$ be the small signal voltages at the
three inverter outputs, Fig. outputs 1,2,3. Let the $i$th
inverter have input $V_{prev}$ and output $V_{i}$.

For the NMOS, $V_{gs}=V_{prev}$, $V_{ds}=V_{i}$,
drain current, drain to source,

$$I_{n}=g_{mn}V_{prev}+\frac{V_{i}}{r_{on}} $$

For the PMOS, source is $V_{x}$, $V_{sg}=V_{x}-V_{prev}$,
$V_{sd}=V_{x}-V_{i}$, source to drain current, neglecting
body effect, the n-well moving with $V_{x}$,

$$I_{p}=g_{mp}(V_{x}-V_{prev})+\frac{V_{x}-V_{i}}{r_{op}} $$

At the output node, at low frequencies, the gate of the
next stage draws no current,

$$I_{p}=I_{n}$$

i.e.

$$g_{mp}(V_{x}-V_{prev})+\frac{V_{x}-V_{i}}{r_{op}}
 = g_{mn}V_{prev}+\frac{V_{i}}{r_{on}} $$

Put

$$\begin{aligned}
G &=\frac1{r_{on}}+\frac1{r_{op}}=\frac1{R_{o}} \\
G_{m}&=g_{mn}+g_{mp} \\
G_{n}&=g_{mn}+\frac1{r_{on}} \\
G_{p}&=g_{mp}+\frac1{r_{op}}
\end{aligned}$$

Then

$$V_{x}G_{p}-V_{prev}G_{m}-V_{i}G=0$$

$$V_{i}G+V_{prev}G_{m}=V_{x}G_{p}$$

For the 3 stage loop:

$$\begin{align*}
V_{1}G+V_{3}G_{m}&=V_{x}G_{p}\\
V_{2}G+V_{1}G_{m}&=V_{x}G_{p}\\
V_{3}G+V_{2}G_{m}&=V_{x}G_{p}
\end{align*}$$

Hence $V_{1}=V_{2}=V_{3}=V$ for the common mode drive.
Indeed summing,

$$(V_{1}+V_{2}+V_{3})(G+G_{m})=3V_{x}G_{p}$$

supply terminal and let the current drawn be $I_{X}$.

$$I_{1}=g_{mP}(V_{X}-V)+\frac{V_{X}-V}{r_{oP}}
      =\big(g_{mP}+g_{oP}\big)(V_{X}-V),$$

$$I_{1}=g_{mN}V+\frac{V}{r_{oN}}
      =\big(g_{mN}+g_{oN}\big)V,$$

with $g_{o}=1/r_{o}$.  Thus one inverter presents, between
supply and ground, the series resistance

$$R_{\text{stage}}=\frac{1}{g_{mP}+g_{oP}}+\frac{1}{g_{mN}+g_{oN}}
   =\left(\frac1{g_{mP}}\Big\Vert r_{oP}\right)
   +\left(\frac1{g_{mN}}\Big\Vert r_{oN}\right),$$

$$V = V_{X}\,
\frac{g_{mP}+g_{oP}}{g_{mN}+g_{oN}+g_{mP}+g_{oP}},\qquad
I_{1}= \frac{(g_{mN}+g_{oN})(g_{mP}+g_{oP})}

$$R_{X}=\frac{V_{X}}{I_{X}}

answer.text:
For a CMOS ring oscillator the supply current that is drawn is almost completely dynamic.

1. Energy needed for one switching event  
 Each inverter charges and discharges its load capacitance CL once every period.  
 Energy per transition E = CL VDD²

2. Average power of an N-stage ring oscillator oscillating at the frequency f  
 Every period each of the N stages switches once, so  

 P = N CL VDD² f

3. Average supply current  
 I = P ⁄ VDD = N CL VDD f                                                 (1)

4. Frequency versus supply voltage  
 The delay of an inverter is approximately  

 tp ≈ k  VDD ⁄ (VDD – VTH)²

 The oscillation period is 2 N tp, therefore  

 f = 1 ⁄ (2 N tp) ≈ (VDD – VTH)² ⁄ (2 N k VDD)

5. Insert f from above into (1)

 I = N CL VDD · (VDD – VTH)² ⁄ (2 N k VDD) = CL (VDD – VTH)² ⁄ (2 k)

 Notice that VDD has canceled out – the average current is (in this simple model) independent of the supply voltage.

6. Small-signal conductance seen from the supply node  

 gx = dI ⁄ dVDD = 0

7. Small-signal resistance  

 Rx = 1 ⁄ gx → ∞

So, to a small-signal (low-frequency) perturbation the ring oscillator looks like an open circuit; the resistance seen looking into its VDD node is essentially infinite.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The answer correctly identifies oscillation-driven capacitive charging and derives the average-current relation, but its frequency-dependent calculation does not make the current independent of VDD: the remaining (VDD−VTH)² term has a nonzero derivative. Thus the infinite-resistance conclusion is wrong.

Let  

VDD = dc supply voltage  
VT  = threshold voltage of the MOS devices  
N   = number of stages in the ring ( N = 3 in the figure )  
CL  = total capacitance that one inverter output drives  
β   = µCox(W/L) of the conducting transistor (the p-device during a 0→1
      transition, the n-device during a 1→0 transition)  
k   ≈ 1 … 1.5 is the constant that appears in the usual delay expression  
( tp ≈ k CL VDD / ION ).

1. Average supply current of the oscillator  

Every node performs one 0→1 and one 1→0 transition each period.  
During a 0→1 transition the supply delivers the charge  

     Q = CL VDD   →   energy Esw = ½ CL VDD².

Therefore the energy drawn from the supply in one period is  

     Ecycle = N · CL VDD² .                                (1)

With oscillation frequency f, the average power is P = Ecycle f and the
average supply current is  

     IDD = P / VDD = N CL VDD f .                          (2)

2. The oscillation frequency as a function of VDD  

For a CMOS inverter

     tp ≈ k CL VDD / ION ,               ION = β (VDD – VT)².     (3)

Hence  

     f = 1/(2N tp) = β (VDD – VT)² /( 2N k CL VDD ).       (4)

3. IDD versus VDD  

Insert (4) into (2):

     IDD(VDD) = N CL VDD · β (VDD – VT)² /( 2N k CL VDD )
              = β (VDD – VT)² /( 2k ).                     (5)

Notice that the load capacitance and the number of stages have dropped
out of the result.

4. Small-signal resistance seen into the supply pin  

     Rx = ( dIDD / dVDD )⁻¹ .

From (5)

     dIDD / dVDD = β (VDD – VT) / k ,

so

     Rx = k / [ β (VDD – VT) ].                            (6)

5. Numerical feel  

For a typical β ≈ 3×10⁻⁴ A/V², VDD – VT ≈ 0.8 V and k ≈ 1,

     Rx ≈ 1 / (3×10⁻⁴ × 0.8) ≈ 4 kΩ.

Thus the 3-stage CMOS ring oscillator presents only a few-kilohm
(positive) small-signal resistance to its supply node, given
approximately by

     Rx ≈ 1 / [ (µ Cox W/L) (VDD – VT) ].

*   **Structure:** The circuit is a ring oscillator composed of three CMOS inverters connected in a loop.
*   **Node $R_x$:** The node labeled $R_x$ is connected to the power supply rail ($V_{DD}$) of the three inverters. The bottom of the inverters is connected to ground (GND).
*   **Signal Path:** The inputs and outputs of the inverters are connected in series (Output of Inverter 1 $\rightarrow$ Input of Inverter 2, etc.).

We need to find the equivalent resistance of the circuit connected to the supply node $V_{DD}$. This means we are looking for the resistance between the supply node and ground as seen from the top terminals of the inverters.

*   **Transistor Modeling:** Each inverter consists of a PMOS transistor connected to $V_{DD}$ and an NMOS transistor connected to GND.
*   **Operating Point:** In a ring oscillator with an odd number of inverters (3 in this case), the circuit is inherently unstable and oscillates. However, for small-signal analysis around a DC bias point (which is typically $V_{DD}/2$ for the signal nodes), we assume the transistors are in the saturation region.
*   **DC/Feedback Path:** The feedback loop connects the output of one inverter to the input (gate) of the next. In DC small-signal analysis (or at low frequencies where gate capacitances are effectively open circuits), the impedance looking into the gate of a MOSFET is very high (infinite). Therefore, no DC small-signal current flows through the feedback loop between the input and output nodes of the gates.
*   **Current Path:** Consequently, the current flowing from the supply node $V_{DD}$ into a single inverter must flow through the PMOS transistor, reach the output node, and then flow through the NMOS transistor to ground. It does not flow through the feedback loop.

**3. Calculating the Resistance**
*   **Resistance of one inverter:** For a single inverter, the resistance looking into the supply ($V_{DD}$) to ground is the series combination of the output resistances of the PMOS and NMOS transistors.
    *   Let $r_{o,p}$ be the small-signal output resistance of the PMOS transistor (often denoted as $r_o$).
    *   Let $r_{o,n}$ be the small-signal output resistance of the NMOS transistor.

To determine the small-signal resistance $R_X$ seen looking into the supply node of the ring oscillator, we analyze the circuit at its DC operating point (the metastable equilibrium point) using a small-signal model.

**1. Circuit Analysis and Operating Point**
The circuit is a 3-stage ring oscillator composed of inverters. For a CMOS ring oscillator, the unstable DC equilibrium point (where small-signal analysis is typically performed) occurs when the input and output of each inverter are at $V_{DD}/2$. At this point, both the NMOS and PMOS transistors in each inverter are in saturation.

**2. Small-Signal Model**
Let's model each inverter stage. The supply node is connected to the source of the PMOS transistor in each inverter. The ground node is connected to the source of the NMOS transistor.
*   Let $g_m$ be the transconductance of the transistors (assuming symmetric inverters where $g_{mn} = g_{mp} = g_m$).
*   Let $r_o$ be the output resistance of the transistors.

We apply a small test voltage $v_x$ at the supply node. We want to find the resulting current $i_x$ flowing into the node, such that $R_X = v_x / i_x$.

**3. Common-Mode Response**
Since the supply voltage $v_x$ is applied to all three stages simultaneously, this is a common-mode perturbation. Due to the symmetry of the ring oscillator, the voltages at the internal nodes (inputs and outputs of the inverters) will all change by the same amount, let's call it $v$.
So, $v_{in,1} = v_{in,2} = v_{in,3} = v_{out,1} = v_{out,2} = v_{out,3} = v$.

For a single inverter stage, the small-signal output voltage $v_{out}$ is related to the input $v_{in}$ and supply $v_x$ by:
$$v_{out} \approx \frac{A_0 + 1}{2} v_x - A_0 v_{in}$$
where $A_0 = g_m r_o$ is the intrinsic gain.
Substituting the common-mode condition $v_{out} = v_{in} = v$:
$$v = \frac{A_0 + 1}{2} v_x - A_0 v$$
$$v(1 + A_0) = v_x \frac{A_0 + 1}{2}$$
$$v = \frac{v_x}{2}$$
This means that for a small change $v_x$ in the supply, the internal node voltages change by $v_x/2$.

**4. Calculating Current and Resistance**
The current $i_x$ drawn from the supply node flows into the sources of the three PMOS transistors.
For one PMOS transistor:
*   Source voltage $v_s = v_x$
*   Gate voltage $v_g = v = v_x/2$
*   Drain voltage $v_d = v = v_x/2$

The small-signal current $i_p$ flowing into the source of the PMOS is:
$$i_p = g_m (v_s - v_g) + \frac{v_s - v_d}{r_o}$$
$$i_p = g_m \left(v_x - \frac{v_x}{2}\right) + \frac{v_x - v_x/2}{r_o}$$
$$i_p = g_m \frac{v_x}{2} + \frac{v_x}{2 r_o} = \frac{v_x}{2} \left(g_m + \frac{1}{r_o}\right)$$

Since there are 3 identical inverters connected in parallel to the supply node, the total current $i_x$ is:
$$i_x = 3 i_p = \frac{3 v_x}{2} \left(g_m + \frac{1}{r_o}\right)$$

The small-signal resistance $R_X$ is:
$$R_X = \frac{v_x}{i_x} = \frac{2}{3 \left(g_m + \frac{1}{r_o}\right)}$$

Assuming $g_m \gg 1/r_o$ (which is typical for MOS transistors, $g_m r_o \gg 1$), the resistance simplifies to:
$$R_X \approx \frac{2}{3 g_m}$$

**Answer:**
The small-signal resistance seen looking into the supply node is approximately **$\frac{2}{3g_m}$** (where $g_m$ is the transconductance of the PMOS transistor in each inverter). If considering the total transconductance of the inverter stage $G_m \approx 2g_m$, it can be written as $\frac{4}{3G_m}$. More precisely, it is $\frac{2}{3(g_m + g_{ds})}$.

## Small‑signal model of one stage

At the bias point of an oscillating ring oscillator each inverter is in its linear region (both devices in saturation). The small‑signal parameters of one inverter are $g_{m_n},g_{m_p},r_{o_n},r_{o_p}$, with output resistance $R=r_{o_n}\parallel r_{o_p}$.

With $v_s$ = small‑signal voltage at the supply node $S$, $v_{in,i}=x_i$ the gate voltage and $v_{out,i}$ the output of stage $i$ (the gate of the next stage, so $v_{out,i}=x_{i+1}$), KCL at the output node gives

$$\left(\tfrac{1}{r_{o_n}}+\tfrac{1}{r_{o_p}}\right)v_{out,i}+(g_{m_n}+g_{m_p})x_i=\left(g_{m_p}+\tfrac{1}{r_{o_p}}\right)v_s$$

Define $a=(g_{m_n}+g_{m_p})R$ (inverter gain magnitude) and $C=(g_{m_p}+1/r_{o_p})R$. Then

$$x_{i+1}=-a\,x_i+C\,v_s$$

## Solving the 3‑stage loop

Adding the three cyclic equations eliminates the individual $x_i$:

$$(1+a)(x_1+x_2+x_3)=3C\,v_s\quad\Rightarrow\quad S\equiv\sum x_i=\frac{3C}{1+a}\,v_s$$

The current drawn from the supply node equals the sum of the NMOS drain currents (the PMOS source currents), so

$$I_S=\sum_i\left(g_{m_n}x_i+\frac{x_{i+1}}{r_{o_n}}\right)=\left(g_{m_n}+\frac{1}{r_{o_n}}\right)S=\frac{3C\left(g_{m_n}+\tfrac{1}{r_{o_n}}\right)}{1+a}\,v_s$$

## Result

$$\boxed{R_x=\frac{v_s}{I_S}=\frac{1+a}{3\,R\left(g_{m_n}+\tfrac{1}{r_{o_n}}\right)\left(g_{m_p}+\tfrac{1}{r_{o_p}}\right)}=\frac{1+A}{3\,R_{out}\left(g_{m_n}+\tfrac{1}{r_{o_n}}\right)\left(g_{m_p}+\tfrac{1}{r_{o_p}}\right)}}$$

where $A=g_m R_{out}$ is the inverter voltage gain.

**Usual approximation** ($g_m r_o\gg1$, i.e. $g_m\gg1/r_o$): the $1/r_o$ terms drop out and $1+a\approx a=g_m R_{out}$, giving a compact result independent of $r_o$:

$$\boxed{R_x \approx \frac{g_{m_n}+g_{m_p}}{3\,g_{m_n}g_{m_p}}=\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{1}{g_{m_n}}+\frac{1}{g_{m_p}}\right)}$$

For a **symmetric** inverter ($g_{m_n}=g_{m_p}=g_m$):

$$R_x \approx \frac{2}{3\,g_m}$$

**Interpretation:** because the three‑stage loop is at the edge of oscillation, the supply perturbation is positively fed back around the ring, increasing the input‑node swings ($S\approx\tfrac{3}{2}v_s$ for a matched stage) and therefore the current pulled from the rail. Hence the oscillator presents a *low* impedance to its supply, on the order of $1/g_m$, much smaller than the inverter output resistance $R_{out}$.

## Setting up the small‑signal model

Linearize each inverter about its symmetric (linear) operating point, $v_{in}=v_{out}=V_M$, where both devices are in saturation. Let the supply node voltage be the test voltage $v_x$, ground be $0$, and let $v_i$ and $v_o$ be the small‑signal input and output of one inverter. (Gate currents are zero, capacitors are open for the low‑frequency incremental resistance.)

**Currents of one inverter**

PMOS (source at $v_x$, gate at $v_i$, drain at $v_o$) – current from the supply node into the PMOS:
$$i_P = g_{mp}(v_x-v_i)+\frac{v_x-v_o}{r_{op}}$$

NMOS (source at 0, gate at $v_i$, drain at $v_o$) – current out of the output node:
$$i_N = g_{mn}\,v_i+\frac{v_o}{r_{on}}$$

**Output‑node KCL** ($i_P=i_N$; the next gate draws no current) gives
$$v_o = K\,v_x - G\,v_i$$
with $R_o=r_{on}\parallel r_{op}$,
$$G=(g_{mn}+g_{mp})R_o,\qquad K=\left(g_{mp}+\tfrac{1}{r_{op}}\right)R_o .$$

## Using the ring feedback

The three inverters form a ring, $v_{o,1}=v_{i,2},\ v_{o,2}=v_{i,3},\ v_{o,3}=v_{i,1}$. The test excitation is symmetric, so the response must be symmetric: $v_{i,1}=v_{i,2}=v_{i,3}=v_i$ and $v_{o,1}=v_{o,2}=v_{o,3}=v_o$. Walking the loop,
$$v_i = K v_x - G v_i\ \Rightarrow\ v_i = \frac{K}{1+G}\,v_x ,$$
and consequently $v_o=v_i\equiv v$.

## Current drawn from the supply node

Only the three PMOS sources are connected to $v_x$, so
$$i_x = 3\,i_P = 3\left(g_{mp}+\tfrac{1}{r_{op}}\right)(v_x-v)
= 3\left(g_{mp}+\tfrac{1}{r_{op}}\right)v_x\,\frac{1+G-K}{1+G} .$$

Hence
$$R_x=\frac{v_x}{i_x}=\frac{1+G}{3\left(g_{mp}+1/r_{op}\right)(1+G-K)} .$$

Substituting $G$ and $K$ and simplifying (note $1+G-K=(g_{mn}+1/r_{on})R_o$ and $1+G=(g_{mp}+1/r_{op}+g_{mn}+1/r_{on})R_o$):

$$\boxed{\,R_x=\frac{1}{3}\left[\frac{1}{g_{mn}+1/r_{on}}+\frac{1}{g_{mp}+1/r_{op}}\right]\,}$$

Equivalently, in terms of the intrinsic gains,
$$R_x=\frac{1}{3}\left[\frac{r_{on}}{1+g_{mn}r_{on}}+\frac{r_{op}}{1+g_{mp}r_{op}}\right].$$

**Neglecting channel‑length modulation** ($r_o\to\infty$):
$$R_x \approx \frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{1}{g_{mn}}+\frac{1}{g_{mp}}\right).$$

This $R_x$ is **positive**: at low frequency the odd number of inverting stages gives negative (stabilizing) feedback around the ring, so a positive increment of $v_x$ draws a positive increment of current. (The *negative* real part that actually sustains the oscillation appears only at the oscillation frequency, where the phase of each inverter deviates from 180°.)

## Setting up the small‑signal test

Place a test source $v_x$ at the supply node (the top rail) and let $i_x$ be the current it must deliver. The small‑signal resistance is $R_x = v_x/i_x$, with all other independent sources zeroed.

Each triangle is an **ideal inverting amplifier**. In its small‑signal model the power‑supply pin does not appear as a node that can carry small‑signal current: the block is a 2‑port (input, output) whose supply pins are, by definition, at AC ground when the model is used. Equivalently, the only small‑signal currents that can enter/leave the block are at the signal pins, and an ideal amplifier draws **no** current at its input.

## Why no current can flow at the supply node

Look at the signal loop. The output of each inverter drives only the *input* of the next inverter, and an ideal inverter input is an open circuit (infinite impedance). Therefore the current that can leave any output terminal is zero, so the inverter's output stage delivers no small‑signal current, and (input current = 0) the small‑signal current through each block's supply terminal is zero.

The closed loop does not change this. Writing the internal node voltages $v_1,v_2,v_3$ around the ring,

$$v_1 = (-A)v_3 = (-A)^2 v_2 = (-A)^3 v_1 \;\Rightarrow\; (1+A^3)v_1 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; v_1=v_2=v_3=0\quad(A>0).$$

So a perturbation applied at the supply cannot sustain any internal signal (the supply node is not part of the gain loop). Hence every small‑signal current that *could* depend on $v_i$ or $v_o$ is identically zero.

The supply node $v_x$ is therefore connected, in the small‑signal equivalent circuit, to **nothing** that can accept current. The test source sees an open circuit:

$$i_x = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{R_x = \dfrac{v_x}{i_x} \to \infty \quad\text{(open circuit)}}$$

Physically: in the ideal inverter model the power supply does not appear in the small‑signal equations, so the supply impedance has no effect on the oscillator's small‑signal (start‑up/oscillation) behaviour.

## Caveat – realistic inverter

If each inverter is instead modelled with a finite small‑signal supply conductance (e.g. a CMOS inverter, where a $v_{DD}$ wiggle modulates the bias current), define $R_p$ = resistance seen at the supply of *one* inverter with its signal terminals at AC ground (for a matched CMOS inverter $R_p \approx 1/g_m$, more exactly $2/(g_m+g_{ds})$ for the unloaded case). Because the three supply currents are independent of each other and the loop cannot transfer supply current into the signal loop, the three $R_p$'s simply appear in parallel at $v_x$:

$$R_x = \frac{R_p}{3} \;\approx\; \frac{1}{3\,g_m}.$$

With the ideal inverting‑amplifier symbols shown in the figure, $R_p=\infty$, recovering $R_x=\infty$.
